title: Perimeter, area, surface area and volume
part: Part IV · Shape, structure and measure
soi: Choosing the right measure—length, area, surface area or volume—connects geometric structure to material use, capacity and cost.
engage: How can a community project estimate turf, paving, fencing, soil and paint without confusing boundary, surface and space?
atl: In order for a student to apply mathematics in real-life contexts, students must select the correct measure, convert units, calculate costs and evaluate a budget with stated assumptions.
objectives: Distinguish perimeter, area, surface area and volume.
Calculate with triangles, quadrilaterals, circles and composites.
Use nets and prism formulas with correct units.
Convert capacity, compare packaging and evaluate a project budget.
vocabulary: perimeter · area · surface area · volume · capacity · radius · diameter · circumference · semicircle · composite · net · prism · cross-section · litre

sections.title: Perimeter and area of triangles and quadrilaterals
sections.intent: Choose the quantity the task needs: boundary length, covered surface or space inside.
paras: Perimeter is the total boundary length. Area measures surface in square units. Rectangle area = length×width; triangle area = ½×base×perpendicular height; parallelogram area = base×height.
A trapezoid with parallel sides a and b and perpendicular height h has area ½(a+b)h. The height must be perpendicular to the parallel sides, not a slant edge.

example.title: A triangle and a trapezoid
example.problem: Triangle: base 8 cm, height 5 cm. Trapezoid: parallel sides 6 and 10 cm, height 4 cm.

sections.warning: Do not use a slant side as the height. Do not report area in cm or perimeter in cm².

practice.prompt: Find the area and perimeter of a 7 cm by 4 cm rectangle.
Find the area of a triangle with base 8 cm and perpendicular height 5 cm.
Find the area of a trapezoid with parallel sides 6 cm and 10 cm and height 4 cm.
A triangle has sides 5, 5, 6 cm. A student uses ½×6×5. Explain the error and find the correct height and area.
practice.answer: The 5 cm side is slant, not perpendicular height. Height is 4 cm; area 12 cm².
practice.reasoning: Half the base is 3; 3–4–5 right triangle.

practice.prompt: A rectangular lawn is 18 m by 12 m. Find its area and the cost of turf at $7.50/m².
A rectangle has area 48 cm² and whole-number sides. Which dimensions give the smallest perimeter?
practice.reasoning: Compare factor pairs of 48; the closest pair minimises perimeter.

verify.expr: min((2*(a+48//a),a,48//a) for a in range(1,49) if 48%a==0)

diagram.caption: Area counts square units (28 cm²); perimeter counts boundary units (22 cm).

sections.title: Circles and composite shapes
sections.intent: Identify radius and diameter, then split a composite shape into familiar pieces.
paras: For a circle, diameter d=2r. Circumference C=πd=2πr; area A=πr². In this chapter use π≈3.14 unless told otherwise, and label results as approximate.
A semicircle has half the circle area and a curved boundary of πr. For a composite plan, add areas of non-overlapping pieces and trace only the outer boundary for fencing.
sections.warning: The diameter is not part of the outer boundary when the semicircle is attached to a rectangle along that edge.

practice.prompt: Find the circumference and area of a circle with radius 5 cm, using π=3.14.
A circle has diameter 12 m. Find its radius, circumference and area (π=3.14).
Find the area and curved boundary of a semicircle of diameter 12 m (π=3.14).
practice.reasoning: Half the circle area; half the circumference.

practice.prompt: An 18 m by 12 m rectangle has a semicircle of diameter 12 m attached to one short end. Find total area and outer boundary (π=3.14).
Why is the 12 m diameter not included in the fencing length of the composite plan?
practice.answer: It is an internal join between lawn and stage, not an outer edge.
practice.reasoning: Fencing follows the outside boundary only.

practice.prompt: If the radius of a circle doubles, what happens to its circumference and area?
practice.answer: Circumference doubles; area becomes four times as large.
practice.reasoning: C is proportional to r; A to r².

diagram.caption: d = 2r. Area uses r²; circumference uses 2r. Use π ≈ 3.14 here.

sections.title: Nets and surface area
sections.intent: A net shows every outside face; surface area adds face areas, not the space inside.
paras: A net is a flat pattern that folds into a solid. The surface area of a closed cuboid is 2(lw+lh+wh). For an open-topped box, omit the top face.
Use square units for surface area. Painting an outside surface depends on area; filling the box depends on volume. Keep the two quantities separate.

example.title: An open-topped raised bed
example.problem: Length 1.2 m, width 0.6 m, height 0.5 m.
steps: Two long sides: 2×1.2×0.5 = 1.20 m². Two short sides: 2×0.6×0.5 = 0.60 m².

sections.warning: A closed cuboid has six faces; an open-topped bed has five. Do not paint an imaginary top.

practice.prompt: Find the surface area of a closed cuboid 4 cm by 3 cm by 2 cm.
Find the surface area of a cube with side 6 cm.
Find the outside area of an open-topped bed 1.2 m by 0.6 m by 0.5 m.
A student uses the closed-cuboid formula for an open box. What must be subtracted?
practice.reasoning: The top is not an outside face to paint.

practice.prompt: Three beds each have outside area 2.52 m². Paint covers 9 m² per litre. How many litres are needed, and how many 1 L tins must be bought?
A cuboid has volume 24 cm³ and whole-number edges. Compare surface areas of 1×1×24 and 2×3×4.
practice.answer: 98 cm² and 52 cm². The compact box uses less material.
practice.reasoning: Same volume does not imply same surface area.

diagram.caption: A net exposes all six faces. Surface area = 2(lw + lh + wh).

sections.title: Prisms, volume and capacity
sections.intent: Volume measures space; capacity measures how much a container can hold.
paras: A prism has a constant cross-section. Volume = cross-section area × length. For a cuboid, V=lwh; for a triangular prism, V=(½×base×height)×length.
Capacity conversions: 1 cm³ = 1 mL; 1,000 cm³ = 1 L; 1 m³ = 1,000 L. Convert units before multiplying or dividing.

example.title: A tank and a prism
example.problem: Tank 50 cm × 30 cm × 40 cm; triangular prism with cross-section base 8 cm, height 5 cm, length 14 cm.

sections.warning: 1 m³ is 1,000 L, not 100 L. Length units scale by 100, area by 10,000 and volume by 1,000,000 between metres and centimetres.

practice.prompt: Find the volume of a cuboid 20 cm by 10 cm by 5 cm.
Find the volume of a triangular prism: cross-section base 8 cm, height 5 cm, length 14 cm.
A tank is 50 cm by 30 cm by 40 cm. Find its capacity in litres.
Convert 2.5 L to cm³, 450 mL to cm³ and 0.8 m³ to litres.
practice.reasoning: Use 1 L=1,000 cm³ and 1 m³=1,000 L.

practice.prompt: A student says 1 m³=100 L because 1 m=100 cm. Correct the reasoning.
practice.answer: 1 m³=1,000,000 cm³=1,000 L. Volume scales in three dimensions.

practice.prompt: A prism has volume 360 cm³ and cross-section area 30 cm². Find its length. If every dimension doubles, what happens to volume?
practice.answer: 12 cm; volume becomes 8 times as large.

diagram.caption: Volume counts cubic units: 5 × 3 × 2 = 30 cm³ = 30 mL.

explore.title: The packaging problem
explore.instruction: Criterion B. Keep volume fixed, compare surface areas, test a second volume and justify a recommendation.
explore.intro: A box has volume 24 cm³ and whole-number edges. Rotations count as the same design. Surface area measures cardboard needed for a closed box.

items.prompt: Complete the surface areas for the six designs.
Which design uses least and most cardboard?
Test volume 27 cm³ with 3×3×3, 1×3×9 and 1×1×27. Does the cube use least?
items.answer: Surface areas 54, 78, 110 cm²; yes, the cube uses least.
items.reasoning: Compact dimensions reduce exposed face area.

items.prompt: Design two closed boxes of volume 36 cm³ and recommend one by material use.
items.answer: Sample: 3×3×4 has area 66 cm²; 1×6×6 has area 96 cm². Recommend 3×3×4 for less cardboard.
items.reasoning: Both volumes are 36; compare surface areas.

items.prompt: Give two practical reasons a manufacturer might not choose the minimum-area box, and one limitation of the pattern.
items.answer: Sample: product shape, stacking, opening strength or shelf display may matter. The pattern compares closed boxes with whole-number edges and ignores waste, tabs and thickness.
items.reasoning: A mathematical optimum is not the only design criterion.

application.title: The courtyard project
application.instruction: Criterion D. Simulated project. Use π=3.14, show units and round purchases up to whole bags or tins.
application.intro: An 18 m by 12 m rectangular lawn has a semicircular stage of diameter 12 m attached to one short end. Three open-topped beds are 1.2 m × 0.6 m × 0.5 m, filled to 80%. Budget $6,000.

items.prompt: Find lawn area, stage area and total area.
items.reasoning: Rectangle plus semicircle of radius 6 m.

items.prompt: Find fencing length and the costs of turf, paving and fencing.
items.reasoning: Boundary 18+18+12+18.84; multiply each quantity by its price.

items.prompt: Find soil needed for three beds and the number and cost of 40 L bags.
items.reasoning: One bed 0.36 m³=360 L; 80% is 288 L; three beds 864 L; ceil(864/40)=22.

items.prompt: Find paint needed for the three open beds and the tin cost.
items.answer: 7.56 m² outside area; 0.84 L paint; buy 1 tin for $22.
items.reasoning: One bed 2.52 m²; three beds 7.56; divide by 9 and round tins up.

items.prompt: Find the total cost and budget position. Then add 10% contingency and state the new position.
items.answer: $6,096.36, over by $96.36. With 10% contingency: $6,706.00 (to the nearest cent), over by $706.00.

assessment.title: The measure explainer
assessment.instruction: Criteria A and C. Explain which measure a purchase needs and check units with a small example.
assessment.intro: A learner confuses perimeter, area, surface area and volume. Use a 4 cm by 3 cm by 2 cm box to make the distinctions clear.

items.prompt: Find the box volume and closed surface area, with units.
Which measure determines cardboard, paint and filling?
items.answer: Cardboard and paint use surface area; filling uses volume or capacity.

items.prompt: Write a unit-check warning and one conversion fact.
items.answer: Sample: “Area uses square units, volume cubic units; 1,000 cm³ = 1 L.”
items.reasoning: Units reveal whether a formula matches the quantity.

groups.title: Mixed practice 9
groups.instruction: Connect ideas. Give units and reasons where requested.

items.prompt: Find the area of a parallelogram with base 9 cm and height 4 cm.

A student uses a slant side as triangle height. Explain the correction.
items.answer: Use the perpendicular distance from the base to the opposite vertex; a slant side is not the height unless it is perpendicular.

items.prompt: A semicircle has radius 4 m. Find its area and curved boundary (π=3.14).

If all lengths of a solid double, what happens to surface area and volume?
